# Deployment Models

Dimension covering sidecar, embedded, library, and WASM deployment options for OPA,
with latency, operational, and failure-mode trade-offs. Sources: [citations.md](../citations.md).

## Deployment Options Overview

OPA supports four primary deployment models [4]:

| Model | Performance | Language Support | Management |
|---|---|---|---|
| REST API (sidecar/daemon) | Fast | Any | Automatic (bundles, logs, status) |
| Go Library | Faster | Go only | Manual implementation required |
| WebAssembly | Fastest | Any with WASM runtime | SDK-dependent |
| IR (Intermediate Representation) | Varies | Custom compilers | Custom |

## Sidecar / Daemon Deployment

The most common pattern: OPA runs as a sidecar container or host-level daemon
alongside the application [4]. Policy decisions are "fast and highly-available"
through local deployment [4].

**Latency**: 2-5ms per authorization decision when co-located (est. from search
snippets — full article inaccessible) [27]. Serial calls across 10 microservices
= 50ms total latency budget (est.) [27].

**Resource requirements**: Production minimum 1 vCPU, 512MB memory (discovery
agent report, unverified — no citation available).

**Failure modes**: Network fault tolerant — continues operating during network
partitions [55]. Centralized deployments face a dilemma: fail-open (DoS grants
full access) or fail-closed (cascade failures) [55].

**AWS guidance**: Centralized deployment suits non-latency-sensitive workloads with
pooled SaaS models. Distributed/sidecar suits latency-sensitive workloads with
siloed SaaS models providing natural tenant isolation [16].

## Embedded Go Library

Using the `rego` package for in-process evaluation eliminates inter-process
latency [4]. The Go SDK provides:
- `sdk.New()` with configuration, `Decision()` method for high-level use
- Lower-level: `PrepareForEval()` then `Eval()` with input data
- Prepared queries are safe to share across Go routines [4]

**Trade-off**: Go-only, requires re-vendoring/redeploying for OPA updates [4].
Automatic management features (bundles, logs, status) require manual implementation [4].

**Miro case study**: Even "tens of milliseconds" was too slow, required in-process
integration for <10ms latency requirement [38].

## WebAssembly (WASM)

OPA compiles Rego to WASM via `opa build` [32]. Claimed as "Fastest" in OPA's own
comparison table [4]. SDKs available for JavaScript (@open-policy-agent/opa-wasm),
Go, and 7+ community SDKs [32].

**Performance reality is mixed** [29]:
- One benchmark: native Rego 1229ms vs WASM 2740ms for 5000 rules
- Another: Rego with indexing 4x faster than WASM for 200 rules (~23,882 ns/op)
- Indexing effectiveness is the key variable — WASM does not benefit from OPA's
  indexing optimizations

## Python Library Options

| Library | Type | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| fastapi-opa [18] | FastAPI middleware | Active (v2.0.3, Jan 2025) | GPLv3+, OIDC/SAML/API Key, 8 contributors |
| opa-python [36] | HTTP client for OPA REST | Inactive | 174 weekly downloads, Python >=3.10, MIT |
| regorus [9] | Rust Rego engine with Python bindings | Active | 10x faster than OPA, not on PyPI officially |
| OPAL [14][37] | Policy administration layer | Active | FastAPI-based, production at Tesla/Walmart/NBA |
| opa-python-client | Sync/async OPA client | Active | Generic Python client |

**Regorus** (Microsoft) benchmarks at 4.6ms ± 0.2ms vs OPA's 45.2ms ± 0.6ms on the
ACI test suite — a ~10x speedup [9]. It passes all non-builtin tests for OPA v1.2.0
but lacks JWT, CIDR, GraphQL, and crypto builtins [9]. Python bindings exist via
pyo3/maturin but are not officially published on PyPI [9].

## Centralized vs Distributed

| Aspect | Centralized | Distributed (Sidecar) |
|---|---|---|
| Latency | Higher (network call) | Lower (local) [16] |
| Tenant isolation | Must enforce in policy [16] | Natural isolation [16] |
| Deployment complexity | Simple [16] | Complex [16] |
| Maintenance | Minimal (single instance) [16] | Significant (all instances) [16] |
| Updates | Easy (centralized) [16] | Difficult (must update all) [16] |
| Failure mode | Single point of failure [55] | Survives partitions [55] |

## Memory Considerations

- Raw JSON to in-memory: approximately 20x the serialized size [2]
- 8MB JSON (100k permission objects) = ~160MB RAM [2]
- OPA data structures = 6x raw JSON size [30]
- Bundle loading times scale non-linearly [30]:
  - 100MB: 16s
  - 200MB: 71s
  - 500MB: 690s (95%+ allocations from recursive data merging)

## Gaps and Limitations

- No independent benchmarks comparing sidecar vs embedded vs WASM under identical
  conditions with realistic API authorization policies
- fastapi-opa has GPLv3+ license which may be incompatible with some projects
- regorus Python bindings lack official PyPI publication — only third-party forks
- WASM performance data is user-reported from GitHub issues, not controlled benchmarks
- Specific p50/p99/p999 latency percentile distributions not available for sidecar
  deployment
